paras: The Bay Minette manhunt and arrest of Keyser Brown was an August 1910 pursuit by armed Alabama posses of Black turpentine workers accused of killing Bay Minette's marshal, ending with Brown's capture near Muscogee, Florida, on August 22. Brown was already wounded by gunshots, and Pensacola officers held him for five days because they expected him to be lynched in Baldwin County. The deputy who arrested him also beat two Black men named Perdue near Muscogee and was dismissed and arrested.

According to the Montgomery Advertiser, Town Marshal Joseph Smith of Bay Minette was shot dead on the evening of August 17 after a white woman telephoned for him to drive away three Black turpentine hands "lounging" near her house. A later report spoke of two men, the larger of whom fired; Bob Morgan, a Black man held after the shooting, named him "Keyser" and the other "Sidney."

Posses put at 200 to "fully 250" men searched Baldwin County with bloodhounds, Black men were taken from trains and jailed, and the Advertiser's correspondent wrote that the fugitives would be "riddled with bullets if seen." A Mobile dispatch in the Richmond Times-Dispatch said a "triple lynching" was "almost certain" to follow a capture.

On August 21 Pensacola police arrested Oscar Moore, whom about twenty possemen "bent upon capturing and lynching" the fugitives promptly identified, according to an Associated Press dispatch. J. B. Graham, a turpentine operator in the Pensacola jail on a federal peonage sentence, recognized the description as that of Keyser Brown and Sydney Hunter, his former workers.

On the morning of August 22 Deputy Sheriff S. T. Andrews and about fifteen Bay Minette men found Brown asleep in a shack at a turpentine camp near Muscogee and handcuffed him; the Advertiser said he "showed fight." He had wounds in the side and back and a charge of bird shot, which the Pensacola Journal said came "probably" from a searching party. Brown was reported to admit being with Hunter but to say Hunter fired, and he was lodged in the Pensacola jail that night.

Sheriff Van Pelt persuaded the Bay Minette men to leave Brown in Florida, and on August 23 the Baldwin County sheriff and thirty or more men left after Pensacola officers warned he "would be lynched and probably a number of other lives lost." That night, after reports of a mob forming near Muscogee and of six automobiles leaving Bay Minette, the sheriff hid the Perdues and strengthened the jail guard; no mob appeared. On August 27 Van Pelt handed Brown to Sheriff Booth of Baldwin County, who took him to the Mobile jail because Bay Minette's was "only a frail affair." Hunter was still at large when coverage ends; no report of a trial was found.

Andrews had also arrested E. C. (or E. R.) and John Perdue, accused of attempting to assault Mrs. Julia Middleton near Muscogee, and by his own account clubbed one with his pistol, cutting his scalp. Van Pelt dismissed him the next day, saying Middleton had "very emphatically" told Andrews they were not the men, and told the Perdues they were free to go. On August 27 Andrews was arrested on a charge, brought by the Perdues' father, of beating the handcuffed men, and gave $200 bond.

The coverage found comes from white dailies, chiefly the Pensacola Journal and the Montgomery Advertiser, with wire versions elsewhere; no Black-press report was found. Alabama reports mourned a "brave officer" and treated lynching as the expected end of the hunt: "Three Lynchings Will Follow Their Capture."

The Pensacola Journal praised the "splendid work" of local officers and backed the sheriff against the posse. On the Perdues it reversed itself within a day, first printing Andrews's claim and then the sheriff's verdict that his statements were "a tissue of falsehoods" and a view that he had tried "to start a race riot."

Brown blamed Hunter for the shooting, while an early report named the larger man, "Keyser," and Alabama authorities were later said to hold Brown responsible. The Journal attributed Brown's wounds to a searching party, whereas the Advertiser placed them at Dyas the night after the killing without naming who fired.

reader.title: Bay Minette manhunt and arrest of Keyser Brown
bases: Armed posses from Bay Minette pursued Black men accused of killing a marshal with a lynching openly predicted (A2, A3, A6); Brown was found shot, 'probably by a searching party' (A9), and was kept in Pensacola because officers expected him to be lynched (A13, A14).

The Pensacola Journal's local reports (A9, A11, A16) and the Montgomery Advertiser's specials (A3, A8, A13, A21), with AP and other wire versions (A2, A6, A14), agree on the killing, the manhunt, Brown's arrest and the lynching fears.

framing.detail: The Montgomery Advertiser praised the 'brave officer' and printed lynching predictions, while its Pensacola specials reported officers' efforts to prevent a lynching.
Wire versions in the Times Dispatch ('Three Lynchings Will Follow Their Capture') and Age-Herald reported the lynching intent as settled expectation.

The Pensacola Journal praised the 'splendid work' of officers in capturing Brown and backed the sheriff against the posse, then denounced Andrews's conduct toward the Perdues as a 'tissue of falsehoods' and an apparent attempt to start a race riot.
